newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Arafat between Israeli hammer and domestic anvil.
newsitem.headline: Arafat between Israeli hammer and domestic anvil.

text.p: Palestinian President Yasser Arafat, caught between an Israeli hammer and a domestic anvil, gave no immediate indication of how he would respond.

After a bloody suicide attack in an Israeli market, the Jewish state suspended talks with the PLO, confined Palestinians to their home districts and demanded that Arafat must crack down on Islamic militants and arrest his police chief.
Arafat was already under fire from Palestinian legislators over allegations of rampant corruption and misrule in his self-rule administration.

Sixteen out of Arafat's 18 ministers offered on Friday to resign after the Palestinian Legislative Council gave Arafat one month in a non-binding vote to dissolve his cabinet and name a new team of "qualified and experienced ministers."
The overwhelming vote followed a scathing report from a panel of nine legislators detailing instances of alleged corruption and squandering of funds.
"If our resignation at this time will serve the Palestinian situation and the Palestinian Authority, we can resign at this moment," Transport Minister Ali al-Qawasmeh told Reuters.
One minister, Arafat confidante Yasser Abed Rabbo, refused to offer to resign and a second, Planning Minister Nabil Shaath, did not attend the cabinet meeting in Ramallah.

Arafat's office confirmed the resignation offers but declined to give further details and was not clear if Arafat, eager to shore up popular legitimacy in view of Israel's clampdown, would accept the resignations.
He has previously indicated that he is prepared to reshuffle his cabinet but Qawasmeh said he doubted if the Palestinian leader would act now.
"No resignations at this time because...we must be united against in front of the Israeli measures," he said.

Arafat was due to go to Egypt on Saturday to consult President Hosni Mubarak on the crisis in Middle East peacemaking since two Arab bombers killed 13 people in the Jerusalem market attack on Wednesday.

"The Palestinian Authority and President Arafat have denounced the recent explosions and pledged to do everything possible and exert every possible effort to prevent such an occurrence from happening," PLO negotiator Saeb Erekat told reporters after the four-hour cabinet meeting.
"Unfortunately (Israeli Prime Minister) Netanyahu instead of declaring war on the enemies of peace, he has declared a war against the Palestinian people and the Palestinian Authority."
The Israeli army said it had rounded up 79 suspected Islamic militants since Wednesday's attack. Palestine Liberation Organisation forces also made arrests in areas under their security control.
Israeli Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai said Palestinian forces had begun to act to a certain extent but not with "full intensity".
"If they want to move forward with us in the (peace) process, they need to meet their basic commitment to fight terror," he told Israel's Channel Two television.
Israel has tightened security as a precaution against further bloodshed. Islamist militants have in the past carried out a series of suicide bombings over several days.
Mordechai said Israel had not yet identified the two bombers but the militant Islamist group Hamas was responsible.

Israel's demands on Arafat came as resentment among ordinary Palestinians grappling with economic hardship deepened over evidence of apparent corruption and mismanagement by Palestinian Authority ministers and officials.

A senior official from the donor community said the International Monetary Fund had urged Arafat to make cabinet changes so that foreign aid, which has totalled some $1.5 billion since 1993, could continue to flow in.
"Domestic discontent grew into resentment and Arafat needs a domestic base so it was natural for him to have some kind of changes," the official said. "He needed to shake the tree."
In Washington, U.S. President Bill Clinton said he would send his Middle East peace envoy Dennis Ross to the region once Israel had finished mourning the victims of Wednesday's bombing.
